# Running the nf-core/rnaseq pipeline v3.23.0

Processing the whole dataset needs more compute than we have in a classroom, so
for the hands-on run we use six *Staphylococcus aureus* USA-100 samples,
sub-sampled to 50,000 reads each: three biofilm and three planktonic, all at the
24 hour time point. The sub-sampling script is `util/subsample_50k_PRJNA685119_GSE163153_Sareus.sh`.

We use pipeline release [v3.23.0](https://nf-co.re/rnaseq/3.23.0). From this
release you can align with Bowtie2, which suits bacterial RNA-seq because
bacteria have no introns and a splice-aware aligner is unnecessary. The
`prokaryotic` profile selects Bowtie2 for alignment and Salmon for
quantification, so we do not have to set those separately.

**To process the data, run the following command:**

```bash
nextflow run 'https://github.com/nf-core/rnaseq' \
    -name 'saureus_usa100_PRJNA685119_GSE163153' \
    -r 3.23.0 \
    -profile prokaryotic,docker \
    --input  '/workspaces/dsp_transcriptomics_27200-Data-driven-bioengineering/data/seq_files_subsampled/PRJNA685119_GSE163153_saureus/usa100/samplesheet_PRJNA685119_usa100_subset_24h.csv' \
    --outdir '/workspaces/dsp_transcriptomics_27200-Data-driven-bioengineering/results/saureus_usa100_nfcore_processing_downsampled' \
    --fasta  '/workspaces/dsp_transcriptomics_27200-Data-driven-bioengineering/data/genome_files/saureus/usa100_NC_002745/GCF_000009645.1_ASM964v1_genomic.fna.gz' \
    --gtf    '/workspaces/dsp_transcriptomics_27200-Data-driven-bioengineering/data/genome_files/saureus/usa100_NC_002745/GCF_000009645.1_ASM964v1_genomic.gtf.gz' \
    -c /workspaces/dsp_transcriptomics_27200-Data-driven-bioengineering/01_scripts/custom.config
```

**What the arguments mean:**

-   `-name`: a name for this run
-   `-r`: which release of the pipeline to use
-   `-profile`: `prokaryotic` (Bowtie2 + Salmon) running in `docker`
-   `--input`: the sample sheet, listing each sample and its two fastq files
-   `--outdir`: where results go (the folder is created for you)
-   `--fasta`: the genome sequence
-   `--gtf`: the genome annotation
-   `-c`: a small config file that caps CPUs and memory so the run fits in a Codespace

The same command is saved as a script, if you prefer to run it that way:

```bash
bash 01_scripts/00_nfcore_rnaseq_processing_saureus.sh
```

It takes about 10 minutes.

<div class="remember">
  <strong>📌 Remember:</strong> You can also set parameters through the nf-core website instead of typing them.
  Go to the [pipeline page](https://nf-co.re/rnaseq/3.23.0), press **Launch version 3.23.0**, fill in the form,
  and it generates a config file you can pass to Nextflow.
</div>

<div class="note">
  <strong>📘 Note:</strong> The counts you analyse in the next chapters were made with this same pipeline, but
  on the full dataset rather than these sub-sampled reads: all three time points for both <em>S. aureus</em>
  strains, and the human samples with STAR instead of Bowtie2 (human genes do have introns). Those outputs are
  already in the repository, so you do not have to run anything before starting the analysis.
</div>

## Structure of the output directory

Results are written to `results/saureus_usa100_nfcore_processing_downsampled`.
The top level looks like this:

```
.
├── bowtie2_salmon
├── fastqc
├── fq_lint
├── multiqc
├── pipeline_info
└── trimgalore
```

What each folder holds:

-   **`bowtie2_salmon`** — the important one. Alignments (`.bam`), per-sample Salmon quantification, and the merged count matrices for the whole run. `salmon.merged.gene_counts.tsv` and `salmon.merged.gene.SummarizedExperiment.rds` are what an analysis like the next chapter starts from.
-   **`fastqc`** — read quality reports, before (`raw`) and after (`trim`) trimming.
-   **`fq_lint`** — format checks on the fastq files.
-   **`multiqc`** — everything above gathered into one report. Start here.
-   **`pipeline_info`** — what ran, for how long, with which software versions. This is your reproducibility record.
-   **`trimgalore`** — adapter and quality trimming reports.

A closer look inside `bowtie2_salmon`, for one sample:

```
bowtie2_salmon
├── USA100_N315_Biofilm_24h_1/          # per-sample Salmon output
│   ├── quant.sf                        #   transcript-level estimates
│   └── quant.genes.sf                  #   gene-level estimates
├── USA100_N315_Biofilm_24h_1.markdup.sorted.bam
├── log/                                # Bowtie2 alignment logs
├── samtools_stats/                     # alignment summaries per sample
├── picard_metrics/                     # duplication metrics
├── deseq2_qc/                          # a quick PCA and sample distances
├── salmon.merged.gene_counts.tsv       # merged counts, genes x samples
├── salmon.merged.gene_tpm.tsv          # merged TPM
├── salmon.merged.gene.SummarizedExperiment.rds
└── salmon.merged.tx2gene.tsv           # transcript to gene mapping
```

## Reading the MultiQC report

MultiQC collects the quality metrics from every step into a single page, so you
can compare all samples side by side instead of opening reports one at a time.

Your own run only has six sub-sampled files, which is too little to judge an
experiment by. So we will look at the report from the full USA-100 dataset,
processed before the course:
[MultiQC report, USA-100](https://github.com/biosustain/dsp_transcriptomics_27200-Data-driven-bioengineering/blob/main/data/data-01-Staphylococcus_aureus/USA-100/data-01-Staphylococcus_aureusUSA100_multiqc_report.html).
On GitHub, click **Download raw file** and open it in your browser. In a
Codespace, right-click the file and choose **Open Preview**.

Things worth looking at:

- The general statistics table at the top, one row per sample
- FastQC metrics: read quality, GC content, adapter content, duplication, before and after trimming
- How many reads aligned, per sample
- The PCA and sample-distance heatmap from DESeq2
- Software versions, at the very end

Spend a few minutes going through it. Use the menu on the left to move around.
We will talk about what you found afterwards.

:::boxy
Sample names tell you the strain, the lifestyle and the time point, for example
`USA100_N315_Biofilm_24h_1` is the first biofilm replicate at 24 hours.
:::
